title: America's Demoralized Men, Part II: Lost Pathways, Greater Struggles https://ifstudies.org/report-brief/americas-demoralized-men-part-ii-lost-pathways-greater-struggles
author: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
summary: The second installment of IFS's two-part survey of 2,000 young American men, ages 18-29, documents a stark portrait of social disconnection and psychological distress: nearly half of respondents feel little steady emotional connection to others, 4 in 10 have two or fewer close friends, including 1 in 10 with none, and many report not belonging to anything they'd call a community. The report finds that 72% agree who you know is more important than ability or hard work in getting ahead, and about half believe the American Dream is out of reach no matter how hard they work, yet paradoxically 84% still report having ambitious goals for their future, suggesting frustrated aspiration rather than simple resignation. The authors find institutional embeddedness, marriage, religious participation, schooling, trade credentials, consistently predicts stronger social connection and lower distress, while men most disconnected from those institutions report the highest rates of loneliness, feeling like a failure, and reliance on gambling, gaming, and pornography as coping mechanisms, with daily pornography users and gamblers reporting failure rates well above the sample average. The report concludes that the erosion of institutional pathways to adulthood, rather than any single cause like screens or fatherlessness, is the throughline connecting young men's frustrated ambitions to their reported isolation and distress.
points: The report's central statistical finding, 61% of young men agree they often feel little control over the things that happen to them, and 42% report feeling like a failure, documents psychological distress at a scale the authors term demoralization rather than simple pessimism.

A striking paradox runs through the data: despite widespread belief that who you know matters more than hard work (72% agreement) and that the American Dream is unreachable, 84% of respondents still report having ambitious goals for their future.

Institutional embeddedness is the report's strongest predictor variable: participation in all-male groups during school years raises the odds of having three-plus close friends from 48% to 64%, and married fathers report anxiety, depression, or bipolar symptoms at half the rate of unmarried men without kids.

Daily users of pornography and gambling report feeling like a failure at nearly 1.5 times the overall rate, and both activities correlate with markedly higher loneliness, evidence the authors frame as coping mechanisms that compound rather than relieve distress.
quotes: Demoralized is the term we use to characterize a state of mind reflected in agreement with such self-appraisals as I am inclined to think that I am a failure (43%), and such expressions of powerlessness as I often feel that I have little control over the things that happen to me (61%), and of being found insufficient, such as I never seem to do enough to please people (54%).

In fact, 4 out of 10 young men have two or fewer close friends, which includes 1 in 3 (34%) with one to two close friends and almost 1 in 10 (9%) who report zero close friends. The best predictor of having three or more friends is connection to institutions like marriage, church, and school.
Nearly three-quarters of young men either strongly (27%) or somewhat strongly (45%) endorse this anti-meritocratic belief; just 7% strongly disagree.

But that is not what we found, not even close. Even to the greater-opportunities statement, 75% think it describes them at least somewhat well. Similarly, 81% and 84% of respondents say the same about their capacities and ambition, respectively.

Of those who watch pornography many times a day or more, 43% experience loneliness, 36% feel depressed, and 29% are anxious. Feeling like a failure is also closely tied to these activities. For example, 66% of daily gamblers and 63% of daily pornography watchers, compared to 42% of men as a whole, report feeling like a failure.

The loss of institutionalized pathways and defined roles, and the simultaneous shift of responsibility to individuals to create their own career and life trajectories have introduced a great deal of precariousness into the lives of young men and left them bereft of guidance and structure.

Married men with kids are around half as likely (16%) to have current anxiety, bipolar disorder, or depression as those who are married without kids (31%) and those who are unmarried without kids (31%).
